title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 11 (21/05/2019)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 21 MAY 2019
Subject: The Respondent challenged one of the Arbitrators (appointed by the Claimant)
pursuant to Article 13 of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules 2010.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: Paris, France
Governing Law of Dutch law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to the fact that the Arbitrator: (i) was sitting as arbitrator
in arbitration proceedings between the Parties’ parent companies (the
Parallel Arbitration), where the tribunal had already rendered an award on
the merits; (ii) participated in the drafting of a model agreement on which the
contract in this case was based; (iii) allegedly worked for a law firm (Law Firm
D) that provided relevant services to, and received substantial fees, from the
Claimant’s private equity backers; and (iv) was challenged by an affiliate of the
Respondent in the Parallel Arbitration. The Respondent argued that these
circumstances represented justifiable doubts as to the Arbitrator’s impartiality
and independence in light of Sections 3.1.5, 3.5.2, 3.1.1 and 3.4.4 of the
Orange List of the IBA Conflicts Guidelines.
In deciding the challenge, the LCIA Court applied the UNCITRAL Rules (2010),
the IBA Conflicts Guidelines, and French procedural law relating to the
arbitration as lex arbitri.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
The fact that the Arbitrator sat as arbitrator in another matter involving an
affiliate of a Party and in which a decision had already been rendered, does
not create a risk of prejudgement under French law, particularly where the
arbitration concerned different parties, a different contract and a different
governing law. The fact that both arbitrations were between affiliated parties
does not of itself give rise to a risk of prejudgement and the Respondent failed
to identify precisely what facts and issues were common to both arbitrations.
The allegation of a risk of prejudgement, without any details or precise
identification of the basis of the alleged overlap, is not sufficient to establish
the existence of prejudice or of a prejudgement.
The fact that the contract in this case was based on a model agreement
formulated by the Arbitrator does not make the latter biased as to the validity
of the contractual clauses at issue. The scenario is not covered by Section 3.5.2
of the Orange List of the IBA Conflicts Guidelines, but is rather comparable to

Section 4.1.1 of the Green List. Moreover, the validity of a contract is never
determined in abstracto but depends on the circumstances of the case and
the applicable law.
As the Arbitrator never worked for Law Firm D, but for a law firm associated
with Law Firm D in a particular jurisdiction, which had no involvement with
the Claimant’s private equity funders, and as the Arbitrator’s employment
ended more than three years before the Request for Arbitration was filed, the
Respondent’s allegations on this point were factually incorrect and in any
event would not fall under Section 3.1.1 of the Orange List of the IBA Conflicts
Guidelines.
As challenges have become commonplace in international arbitration, the fact
that the Arbitrator was challenged in the Parallel Arbitration by an affiliate of
the Respondent, does not establish that enmity might exist between the
Arbitrator and the Respondent for purposes of Section 3.4.4 of the Orange List
of the IBA Conflicts Guidelines absent specific evidence to the contrary.
Decision 11 - 2

LCIA Arbitration No: […]
Between
[…]
(CLAIMANT)
And
[…]
(RESPONDENT)
DECISION ON THE CHALLENGE BROUGHT AGAINST
[A]
21 May 2019
Decision 11 - 3

1. By letter dated 21 March 2019, I have been informed that pursuant to Article 13(4) of the UNCITRAL
Rules and Article D.3 (b) of the Constitution of the LCIA Court, I had been appointed by the LCIA Court
to determine a challenge brought by the Respondent in the matter of an UNCITRAL arbitration
between [the] Claimant, and [the Respondent].
The procedure to date
2. A dispute has arisen between the above-named parties out of a shareholders agreement, dated 21
February 2013 and stated to have been made between [the Respondent]; [the Claimant] and [a Third
Party] (the “Shareholders Agreement”);
3. By email dated 11 January 2019, the Claimant sent a Notice of Arbitration, dated 10 January 2019 (the
“Request for Arbitration”), by which it invoked the provisions of Clause 32 of the Shareholders
Agreement (the “Arbitration Clause”), which provides in its relevant parts, as follows:
“Section 32. Governing Law and Dispute Resolution
32.1 This Shareholders Agreement shall be governed and construed in accordance with the laws of
the Netherlands.
32.2 Any dispute, controversy or claim arising out or in relation to in connection (sic) with this
Shareholders Agreement or the operations carried out under this Shareholders Agreement, including
any dispute as to the construction, validity, interpretation, enforceability or breach of this Shareholders
Agreement, shall be exclusively and finally settled by arbitration under this Section 32 in accordance
with the Arbitration rules of the UNCITRAL. Any party hereto may submit such dispute, controversy or
claim to arbitration by written notice to the other parties hereto. The London Court of International
Arbitration (the “Court”) shall administer the arbitration.
32.3 The arbitration shall be heard and determined by three (3) arbitrators. In case of any dispute
between two parties hereto or two groups of parties hereto, each side shall appoint an arbitrator of
its choice, and in case of any dispute among two or more parties hereto, two of the arbitrators shall
be appointed by agreement of the parties involved, in both cases within thirty (30) days of the
submission of a notice of arbitration. The party-appointed arbitrators shall in turn appoint a presiding
arbitrator of the tribunal within thirty (30 days) following the appointment of both party-appointed
arbitrators. If the party-appointed arbitrators cannot reach agreement on a presiding arbitrator of the
tribunal and/or one party refuses to appoint, and/or the parties involved on either side or both sides
of the arbitration are not able to agree upon the appointment of, their party-appointed arbitrator
within said thirty (30) day period, the appointing authority for the implementation of any such
procedures shall be the chairperson (or its equivalent) of the Court, who shall appoint independent
arbitrators who do not have any financial or other interest in the dispute, controversy or claim. All
decisions and awards by the arbitration tribunal shall be made by majority vote.
32.4 Unless otherwise expressly agreed in writing by the parties to the arbitration
proceedings:
a. the arbitration proceedings shall be held in Paris, France;
b. the arbitration proceedings shall be conducted in the English language and the arbitrator(s)
shall be fluent in the English language;
c. the arbitrator(s) shall be and remain at all times wholly independent and impartial;
d. the arbitration proceedings shall be conducted under the Arbitration Rules of the UNCITRAL in
effect on the Effective Date;
Decision 11 - 4

[…]
j. the presiding arbitrator shall not be of the same nationality as any ultimate parent entity of
any party hereto, unless otherwise agreed;
[…]”;
4. As mentioned in Article 32. 4 of the Shareholders Agreement, the seat of the arbitration is Paris, France
and the arbitration is to be conducted under the Uncitral Rules. French procedural law relating to
arbitration is also relevant as it the lex arbitri, as pointed out by Respondent at paragraph 4.2 of its
Challenge of 8 February 2019.
5. In the Request for Arbitration, the Claimant informed the Respondent and the LCIA that it appointed,
as arbitrator, [A].
6. By email of 8 February 2019, the Respondent filed a Response to the Request for Arbitration, to which
it attached a challenge to [A], pursuant to Article 13(4) of the UNCITRAL Rules, dated 25 January 2019
and addressed to the Claimant and [A].
7. By email dated 8 February 2019, the LCIA invited the Claimant to advise whether it agreed to the
challenge.
8. By email dated 10 February 2019, the Claimant attached its email to the Respondent dated 6 February
2019, in which it objected to the challenge.
9. By email dated 12 February 2019, the LCIA invited the challenged arbitrator to advise whether he was
minded to withdraw.
10. By email dated 21 February 2019, the challenged arbitrator refused to withdraw from the arbitration
and submitted his signed statement of independence and availability, in which he disclosed certain
information in relation to his appointment as arbitrator.
11. By email dated 27 February 2019, the LCIA invited the parties’ comments on the challenged
arbitrator’s disclosure by 4 March 2019.
12. By emails dated 4 March 2019, the Respondent maintained its challenge and the Claimant maintained
its objection to the challenge.
The Challenge
13. As mentioned above, the dispute arises out of the Shareholders Agreement dated 21 February 2013
and stated to have been made between [the Respondent], [the Claimant] and [the Third Party].
14. In the Request for Arbitration, the Claimant states that a company affiliated to [itself], a company
affiliated to [the Third Party] and a company affiliated to [the Respondent] were parties to a [number
of agreements] aimed at exploiting, developing and producing hydrocarbons off the coast of [Country
C]. A company named [Company B] was established as part of the […] operations. [The Claimant], [the
Third Party] and [the Respondent] are the sole shareholders of that company.
Decision 11 - 5

15. In its Request, the Claimant states that Clause 7.2 of the Shareholders Agreement stipulates that each
shareholder in [Company B] shall contribute its Respective Proportion share of the estimated cash
requirements for the operations of [Company B] as set forth in a cash call delivered to the
shareholders. The Claimant states that [the Respondent] failed to contribute its share.
16. The Claimant further states that Clause 8.3 of the Shareholders Agreement states that the total of all
amounts paid by the non-defaulting shareholders on behalf of the defaulting shareholder, together
with interest as calculated in accordance with Clause 8.1, shall constitute a debt due and owing by the
defaulting shareholder to the non-defaulting shareholders. As a result, the Claimant states that the
Respondent owes it USD 6,219,208.43 as of 31 December 2018. The Respondent has not yet received
payment of such amount and therefore seeks an award ordering that the Respondent pay this amount.
17. By an email of 8 February 2019, the Respondent filed a Response, in which it denied the Claimant’s
entitlement to any such payments and requested the Tribunal to reject the relief sought by the
Respondent.
18. Two weeks before, on 25 January 2019, a Notice of Challenge was sent by the Respondent to the
Claimant and to [A]. It was not copied to the LCIA. In paragraph 4.5 of the Response to the Request
for Arbitration filed with the LCIA, the Respondent states that the Claimant objected to the challenge
on 6 February 2019. The Respondent therefore applied, in paragraph 4.5 of the Response, for a
decision on the challenge from the Appointing Authority, the LCIA, in accordance with Article 13(4) of
the UNCITRAL Rules.
19. The Respondent bases its challenge on the following circumstances, which the Respondent alleges
represent justifiable doubts as to the impartiality and independence of [A]:
(1) In arbitration proceedings between the parent companies of the Claimant and the Respondent […]
(the “[C] Arbitration”), the Tribunal, on which [A] sits as an arbitrator, has already rendered an award
on the merits of the dispute (“Ground (1)”);
(2)[A] was challenged in the [C] Arbitration in relation to the disclosures he made in that arbitration,
in particular in relation to his participation in the drafting of model agreements with [Group X]. The
Respondent also relies in this challenge on the fact that [A] participated in the drafting of the [Group
X] model contract for [the] Agreement ([Group X] Model [Agreement]). According to the Respondent,
already at this stage of the proceeding, [the Claimant] has raised issues regarding three paragraphs of
the Shareholders Agreement. Each of these paragraphs in turn substantially tracks the language of
provisions from the […] Agreement at issue in the [C] Arbitration, which was based on the [Group X]
Model [Agreement]. The Respondent states that [A] having worked in the drafting of the [Group X]
Model [Agreement] would make him biased to determine the validity of the [Agreement]’s clauses
which were based on that model (“Ground (2)”);
(3)the fact that [A] worked for a firm (Law Firm D]) that provided relevant services to, and received
substantial fees, from the Claimant’s private equity, a fact on which he would not have been fully
transparent in his disclosure in the [C] Arbitration (“Ground (3)”);
Decision 11 - 6

(4)the fact that [A] was challenged by an affiliate of the Respondent means that it will be more difficult
for him to bring an independent mind to a case that allegedly runs a significant risk of overlapping
facts, issues and affiliated parties (“Ground (4)”).
20. By email dated 21 February 2019, [A] confirmed that he intended to accept his appointment in the
present matter, in spite of the challenge, and would not withdraw. He also submitted his statement
of independence and availability, with a disclosure relating to his appointment in the present matter
and his disclosure in the [C] Arbitration. The disclosure reads as follows:
“1. I am an arbitrator in another LCIA administered arbitration […] where the parties are affiliated
companies of the Claimant and the Respondent in this arbitration. I was appointed by an affiliated
company of the Claimant and challenged by an affiliated company of the Respondent in the [C]
arbitration. On [a certain date], all the grounds of challenge brought by the affiliated company of the
Respondent were dismissed and my appointment was confirmed in the [C] arbitration.
2. Even though the parties and counsel in this arbitration are fully aware of the [C] arbitration, my
disclosures in that arbitration, the challenge to my appointment, and the decision confirming my
appointment; in order to ensure full disclosure in this arbitration, I attach all of the disclosures1 I made
in the [C] arbitration.
3. I do not know, nor have I had any past or present relationship with, the other party appointed
arbitrator, [Arbitrator G].
4. I do not believe that any of the above circumstances are in conflict with [this LCIA Arbitration].
However, out of an abundance of caution, I wish to disclose any circumstance that may give rise to the
mind of any party in this LCIA arbitration any justifiable doubt as to my impartiality or independence”.
21. In the [C] arbitration, in which the Claimant’s affiliate is also a party, the Claimant nominated [A]. He
was challenged by the Respondent. By a Challenge Decision […], the challenge was dismissed […]. It is
apparently on the basis of the outcome of the challenge in that related matter that [A] decided not to
withdraw his appointment in the present matter.
22. In an email dated 4 March 2019, the Respondent confirmed its challenge of [A] for the following
reasons:
1 The disclosure was as follows:
Disclosure of Certain Circumstances Prior to Appointment:
1. I have no relationship or conflicts with any of the Parties, in addition to the company/entity referred to in the
Request: [Entity E]. A number of […] subsidiaries of [Company F] previously held an interest in the agreement in
dispute. I was employed by a [foreign] subsidiary of [Company F] [for a certain period]. My understanding is that
neither [Company F] nor any of its subsidiaries are a party to this dispute.
2. I know a number of counsel representing both the Respondents and the Claimant. A number of them have
spoken at [a conference] that I chair each year or I have spoken on or moderated panels at arbitration
conferences on which some of these counsel have participated. In addition, I am a member of professional
organizations, such as [Group X] […], to which some of these counsel are members also. I do not have a close
personal relationship with any of these counsel.
3. I do not know, nor have I had any past or present relationship with, the other party appointed arbitrator,
[Arbitrator H].
4. I do not believe that any of the above circumstances are in conflict with [C Arbitration]. However, out of an
abundance of caution, I wish to disclose any circumstance that may give rise to the mind of any party in this LCIA
arbitration any justifiable doubt as to my impartiality or independence.”
Decision 11 - 7

1. “a crucial reason for the challenge in this matter was always [A]’s participation in the related
arbitration [C Arbitration]. The Respondent highlighted para 3.1.5 of the Orange List: “The arbitrator
currently serves, or has served within the past three years, as arbitrator in another arbitration on a
related issue involving one of the parties, or an affiliate of one of the parties.”
2. "Following [the Respondent’s] Notice of Challenge of [A] on 25 January 2019, [A] subsequently
participated in the rendering of a second award on the merits in [C Arbitration]. [A] has now expressed
his views on issues that cut to the merits of the present case in definitive terms without contemplating
the possibility that his view might change not once but twice".
3. “[A]’s response to the Arbitrator challenge from [C Arbitration] predominantly relates to the timing
and content of his disclosures … rather than the merits of the challenge … no such concerns regarding
such timing exist in the present arbitration”.
4. [A] has expressed an opinion pertaining to the merits of this case, and the precise risk involved in
this situation is prejudgement/predisposition, creating the appearance of bias.
23. In answer, the Claimant, in an email dated 4 March 2019, relied on [the] reasons for rejecting the
challenge in [C Arbitration], namely:
1. The length of time that had elapsed since the end of [A]’s employment with the [Law Firm I2] ([A]
having never worked for [Law Firm D]), the tentative nature of the connection between [A] and the
shareholders of [Company J] and [A]’s lack of knowledge of [Company J] shareholders;
2. [A] did not fail in any material way with his duties of disclosure. Moreover, his past involvement and
familiarity with the […] model form agreements were irrelevant insofar as the challenge was
concerned.
3. The assertions of bias on the part of [A] were unconvincing.
24. In relation to Ground (1) for the challenge in this arbitration, namely that “[A] has already rendered
an award on the merits”, the Claimant noted that “the Respondent itself accepts that this arbitration
concerns different parties, a different contract and a different governing law” (Respondent’s email
dated 11 February 2019 and para. 5.26 of the Challenge […]). Moreover, the Claimant maintains that
the issues presented in this arbitration are not the same.
Analysis and Decision
25. Article 11 of the 2010 UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules provides that:
“When a person is approached in connection with his or her possible appointment as an arbitrator, he
or she shall disclose any circumstances likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to his or her impartiality
or independence. An arbitrator, from the time of his or her appointment and throughout the arbitral
proceedings, shall without delay disclose any such circumstances to the parties and the other
arbitrators unless they have already been informed by him or her of these circumstances.”3
2 This is a […] law firm in which [A] was [a lawyer] [for a certain period]. During that period, the firm had an
alliance with [Law Firm D] (email of January 2, 2019, §4 of [A] and his Statement of 28 January 2019 in relation
to his Challenge in the [C Arbitration], §§3 to 5).
3 Article 1456 of the French Code of Civil Procedure also provides that “[b]efore accepting a mandate, an
arbitrator shall disclose any circumstance that may affect his or her independence or impartiality. He or she also
shall disclose promptly any such circumstance that may arise after accepting the mandate”.
Decision 11 - 8

26. Article 12 further provides in part that:
“1. Any arbitrator may be challenged if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the
arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
…”
27. Article 13 further provides that:
“1. A party that intends to challenge an arbitrator shall send notice of its challenge within 15 days after
it has been notified of the appointment of the challenged arbitrator, or within 15 days after the
circumstances mentioned in articles 11 and 12 became known to that party.
2. The notice of challenge shall be communicated to all other parties, to the arbitrator who is
challenged and to the other arbitrators. The notice of challenge shall state the reasons for the
challenge.
3. When an arbitrator has been challenged by a party, all parties may agree to the challenge. The
arbitrator may also, after the challenge, withdraw from his or her office. In neither case does this imply
acceptance of the validity of the grounds for the challenge.
4. If, within 15 days from the date of the notice of challenge, all parties do not agree to the challenge
or the challenged arbitrator does not withdraw, the party making the challenge may elect to pursue it.
In that case, within 30 days from the date of the notice of challenge, it shall seek a decision on the
challenge by the appointing authority.”
28. According to General Standard 2 of the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts, which are the Standard of the
profession and represent international best practice, and which, moreover, the parties have referred
to in their submissions to justify the challenge or object to it, a challenge may be upheld “if facts or
circumstances exist, or have arisen since the appointment, which, from the point of view of a
reasonable third person having knowledge of the relevant facts and circumstances, would give rise to
justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or independence”.
29. It is to be noted that, as regards Grounds (2) and (3), the challenge is based on the same reasons as
those put forward in the challenge filed in [C Arbitration], which was rejected […]4. Additionally
Grounds (1) and (4) raise new reasons.
30. The Respondent alleges in Ground (2) that the fact that [A] has played a role in the drafting of the
[Group X] Model [Agreement], makes him biased as to the personal belief that the clauses based on
that Model are valid. Respondent invokes in that respect Section 3.5.2 of the IBA Guidelines’ Orange
List which refers to the situation where an arbitrator has publicly advocated a position on the case,
whether in a published paper, or a speech, or otherwise. Contrary to what the Respondent alleges,
the undersigned does not consider that the fact that the Shareholders Agreement tracks the language
of provisions from the […] Agreement that was based on the [Group X] Model [Agreement] and that
[A], as [part] of the Model [Agreement] [committee], was responsible for the development of all
[Group X] Model [Agreements] worldwide, is analogous to the situation referred to in Section 3.5.2.
4 Information communicated to the undersigned by the LCIA Secretariat. The text of the decision […] was not
communicated to the undersigned.
Decision 11 - 9

The situation is rather comparable to the one referred to in the Green List under Section 4.1.1: “The
arbitrator has previously expressed a legal opinion (such as in a law review, article or public lecture)
concerning an issue that also arises in the arbitration (but this opinion is not focussed on the case)”.
Moreover, the validity of a contract is never determined in abstracto but depends on the
circumstances of the case and the applicable law. This ground is therefore unfounded.
31. Respondent also bases its challenge on the fact that because [A] has been challenged in the [C]
Arbitration, enmity might exist between himself and Respondent, as provided in Section 3.4.4 of the
Orange List. This argument is based on speculation. Challenges have become commonplace in
international arbitration. Unless there is specific evidence to the contrary, which is not presented in
this case, there is no reason to believe that because he has been challenged in the [C] Arbitration by
an affiliate of the Respondent, enmity or any kind of antagonism would exist vis-a-vis Respondent in
the mind of [A]. This ground is therefore unfounded.
32. Respondent also invokes as a ground for challenge that [A] worked for [Law Firm D] which maintained
a substantial working relationship with certain of [Company J]’s private equity owners or affiliates of
the owners in the energy market (Ground 3). Section 3.1.1 of the Orange List refers to the situation
where “the arbitrator has, within the past three years, served as counsel for one of the parties, or an
affiliate of one of the parties, or has previously advised or been consulted by the party, or an affiliate
of the party, making the appointment in an unrelated matter, but the arbitrator and the party, or the
affiliate of the party, have no ongoing relationship”. In his statement […] following the challenge in
the [C Arbitration], [A] declared the following:
“1. My first and only knowledge of the Second Respondent’s shareholders was when the Claimant
disclosed [their names] in its letter […] and … in his Challenge of Arbitrator […].
2. Until the Claimant’s disclosures, I had never heard of these two companies. In addition to my
complete lack of knowledge about these two companies, I have never dealt with either of them at any
time. I was also not aware that [Law Firm D] had provided legal services to these two companies until
the Claimant disclosed such information in its challenge.
…
4. I have not been a partner or an employee of [Law Firm D] at any time.
5. As described in the attached letter from [Law Firm I], [the latter] firm was associated with [Law Firm
D] in providing legal services in [Country K] during my employment in [Country K] with [Law Firm I].
During that time period, my work was exclusively focussed on the [regional] clients of [Law Firm I]”.
Moreover, it appears from the record that [A] was only employed by [Law Firm I] [for a certain period],
i.e., more than three years before the filing of the Request for Arbitration. It results from the above
that this ground for challenge is based on factually incorrect allegations and in any case would not fall
under the provision of Section 3.1.1 of the Orange List. It is therefore not founded.
33. Finally, with respect to the situation referred to in Section 3.1.5 of the Orange List, i.e., that [A] has
served as arbitrator in another arbitration involving an affiliate of one of the parties and in which
awards have already been rendered (Ground 1), the issue is to determine whether there is a risk of
prejudgement, as the concept was very well defined by the French Cour de Cassation in its decision of
14 October 1993 (1994 Rev. Arb., 380 and following): “An unfavourable prejudice, particularly if the
arbitrator has participated in the first case, in an award which logically carries certain consequences
on the questions to be decided in the second; however, this prejudice must have a bearing on the
indissociable whole of fact and law which constitutes the substance of the matter submitted to
Decision 11 - 10

arbitration ; indeed, there is neither prevention nor prejudice when the arbitrator is called to give his
decision on a factual situation similar to the one examined before, but between different parties, and
even less so when he must decide an issue of law which he has previously decided”.
34. The Respondent has not convincingly established that there was such a risk of prejudgement in the
present case. As previously noted, the Respondent has recognised that this arbitration concerns
different parties, a different contract and a different governing law. It has referred to a “significant
risk of overlapping facts, issues and affiliated parties” (Challenge, sections 5.18 and 5.25), without
giving any explanation or details of what precisely the alleged overlap is said to relate to. The fact of
both arbitrations being between affiliated parties does not of itself give rise to a risk of prejudgement
and the Respondent has not identified precisely what facts and issues it says are common to both
arbitrations. For its part, the Claimant has submitted that the issues presented in this arbitration are
not the same as those in the [C] Arbitration (email of 4 March 2019). The allegation of a risk, without
any details or precise identification of the basis of the alleged overlap, is not sufficient to establish the
existence of prejudice or of a prejudgement. This is particularly so where it is common ground that
this arbitration concerns different parties, a different contract and a different governing law. This
ground is therefore unfounded.
35. In conclusion, and for the reasons given above, I do not consider that circumstances have been
established that, in the mind of a reasonable third person having knowledge of the relevant facts and
circumstances, would give rise to justifiable doubts as to [A]’s impartiality or independence.
Accordingly the test for challenging [A] under Article 12 of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules has not
been met. The challenge is therefore dismissed.
36. The costs of the challenge amount to GBP 7,502 (VAT included) being the fees of the undersigned and
GBP 7,619.06 being the charges (VAT included) that the LCIA has incurred for dealing with the
challenge, that is a total of GBP 15,121.06 (VAT included). They have to be borne by Respondent.
[…]
Decision 11 - 11
